title: The History of Super Smash Bros | From Nintendo 64 To Ultimate And Sora | Gaming History
description: The history of Super Smash Bros: Masahiro Sakurai and HAL, the Nintendo 64 original in 1999, Melee, Brawl, the 3DS and Wii U games, Ultimate in 2018 and Sora as the final fighter in 2021.

sections.heading: The crossover that shouldn't work
sections.script: Welcome back to the channel. Today we are going through the history of Super Smash Bros, the series where Mario, Link, Pikachu and many other famous characters from different games fight on the same stage. It sounds like a strange idea, but it turned into one of Nintendo's biggest series. We will start with the creator, Masahiro Sakurai, and the Nintendo sixty four original in nineteen ninety nine, then go through Melee, Brawl, the games on three DS and Wii U, and Super Smash Bros Ultimate, which brought nearly everyone back together. We will finish with the surprise that closed the series' downloadable content in twenty twenty one. Every date comes from Wikipedia and from news coverage and official pages. Let us jump into the first match.

sections.heading: Masahiro Sakurai's idea
sections.script: The series was created by Masahiro Sakurai, who was working at the studio HAL Laboratory in the nineties. He wanted to make a fighting game that was friendly and easy to pick up, and he used Nintendo characters because players already knew and loved them. According to Wikipedia, he developed the idea in the second half of the nineties, with help from the late Satoru Iwata, who was then a programmer at HAL and later became Nintendo's president. The first version was a test with just a few characters. From that small start, the idea grew into a full game that Nintendo released on its console.

sections.heading: Super Smash Bros on Nintendo 64
sections.script: Super Smash Bros was released for the Nintendo sixty four in Japan on the twenty first of January, nineteen ninety nine, and in North America on the twenty sixth of April, nineteen ninety nine. It had a small roster of famous Nintendo characters, and instead of health bars, it used a percentage that went up when you were hit. The higher the number, the further you flew when someone hit you, and the goal was to knock your opponent off the stage. Four players could play at once, and the simple controls let anybody join in. It was a very different kind of fighting game, and it was a success that made a sequel certain.

sections.heading: Melee on GameCube
sections.script: The sequel, Super Smash Bros Melee, came to the GameCube. It was released in Japan on the twenty first of November, two thousand one, and in North America on the third of December, two thousand one. Sakurai led the project again at HAL. Melee was faster and deeper than the original, with many more characters and modes, and it became a favourite of competitive players who still organise tournaments for it today. It gave the GameCube a very strong title. Many fans still call it their favourite, and that shows how much of an impression a fast, expressive fighting game can leave.

sections.heading: Brawl on Wii
sections.script: The third game, Super Smash Bros Brawl, launched in twenty oh eight on the Wii. Its release dates were the thirty first of January in Japan and the ninth of March in North America. Satoru Iwata asked Sakurai to create it, and Sakurai led the development with a team that was gathered from several studios. Brawl was bigger in scale than its predecessors, with guest characters from outside Nintendo and a large story mode, and it let players take the series online for the first time. It was a very ambitious entry, and the work behind it showed how big the project had become.

sections.heading: Two games in twenty fourteen
sections.script: In twenty fourteen, the series came out on two systems at once. Super Smash Bros for Nintendo three DS was released in Japan on the thirteenth of September and in North America on the third of October, twenty fourteen, and the Wii U version followed in North America on the twenty first of November. This gave players one game they could carry in their pocket and another for the living room. The Wii U version used the console's high definition graphics, while the three DS version could be played anywhere. The two games shared much of the same roster, which made them feel like partners, and they kept the series going between consoles.

sections.heading: Ultimate on Nintendo Switch
sections.script: Then came Super Smash Bros Ultimate on the Nintendo Switch, released worldwide in December twenty eighteen. Its big promise was that everyone is here, bringing back every fighter from the earlier games in a single package, together with new ones. It was a celebration of the whole series, and it turned into a major seller for Nintendo. Players could use it at home on the television, take it on the go and play it with friends, and the large roster meant that fans of almost any Nintendo game could find their favourite character. Wikipedia lists the series as having more than eighty fighters in total, which shows how far the idea had grown from the first small roster.

sections.heading: Guest fighters and downloadable content
sections.script: After launch, Ultimate kept growing through downloadable fighters. The game added characters from outside Nintendo's own games, which is one of the things that always made Smash special. Each new announcement became a big event for fans, often made through a special presentation by Sakurai himself. This is a good example of the way the series keeps its community involved: the characters are chosen with the help of a lot of fan excitement, and every reveal is a chance for players around the world to talk about what they hope to see. The final announcement was the biggest one, and it showed that the series still had a surprise in store.

sections.heading: Sora joins as the final fighter
sections.script: On the fifth of October, twenty twenty one, Sakurai revealed in the last presentation of the series that the final fighter for Ultimate would be Sora from Kingdom Hearts. Reports at the time said Sora was the most requested new character in a fan survey from the three DS and Wii U era. He launched on the eighteenth of October, twenty twenty one, as part of the second Fighters Pass, and could also be bought alone. Sakurai said there would be no more Fighter Passes, so Sora is the last downloadable fighter. It was a surprise to many fans, and for a lot of people, it was the perfect ending to the content for the game.

sections.heading: Why Smash lasts
sections.script: So why has Super Smash Bros lasted for more than twenty five years? One answer is that it is a party game that anybody can play, since the controls are simple and the damage meter makes every fight a fresh story. Another answer is that it is a love letter to many different games. Every character brings a piece of gaming history, and every stage is a memory for somebody. And the third answer is the competitive scene, where players take the same game to a very deep level. Few series can be both a friendly party game and a serious tournament game at the same time, but Smash has always managed to be both.

sections.heading: Your favourite Smash game
sections.script: That was the history of Super Smash Bros, from the Nintendo sixty four original in nineteen ninety nine to Sora joining Ultimate in twenty twenty one. Now we want to hear from you. Which Smash game is your favourite, and who is the character you always pick? Are you a Melee fan, a Brawl fan or an Ultimate fan? And which character would you most like to see in a future game? Tell us in the comments below. If you enjoyed this history, subscribe to the channel and turn on notifications, because we have many more franchise histories coming up.
